idiom_name: optional-interface visitor protocol: comma-ok assertion with a default fallback (embedding for defaults)
implementation_notes: Go rebuilds the protocol from optional interfaces: the visitor is an interface with a default method, an extended visitor is a second interface that embeds the first and declares one method per new element kind, and the new element negotiates with a comma-ok type assertion - `if uv, ok := v.(UnionVisitor); ok { uv.VisitUnion(u); return }; v.VisitDefault(u)` - the same idiom the standard library uses to detect optional capabilities such as io.StringWriter and http.Flusher on an io.Writer. Go interfaces cannot carry method bodies, so the default behaviour lives in a struct that visitors embed (`BaseVisitor` with a VisitDefault method) and extending an existing visitor means embedding its struct and overriding methods: composition takes the place of the implementation inheritance the pattern normally pays with. A closed element set should not use this at all - one function with a type switch over the variants is smaller, faster and needs no negotiation.
pitfalls: Interfaces have no method bodies, so every visitor must supply the default method - embed a base struct carrying it, or the type simply does not satisfy the protocol.

Wrapping a visitor in another interface-typed value hides the extended interface: the comma-ok assertion then fails silently and the default path runs, the same trap that makes io.StringWriter fast paths disappear behind wrappers.
A failed assertion without `, ok` panics, and in the comma-ok form the first result is the zero value: never keep using the asserted value after a failed check.

The interface set of a type is structural, so a visitor accidentally satisfying an extended interface (same method name and signature) is treated as one - name visitor methods with the element kind to keep accidental satisfaction unlikely.
